name: Market Volatility and Volume
description: During high-volatility events (e.g., CPI releases, central bank rate decisions), the volume of market ticks spikes drastically. Since Technical Analysis (TA) processes tick data, execution times naturally form distinct clusters corresponding to low, medium, and high volatility periods.

name: Data Cache Hit Rate
description: A classic source of bimodal/multimodal performance. If market data, order books, or historical rates are cached locally (warm cache), TA runs extremely fast. If the cache expires or is invalidated (cold cache), the workflow must query the primary database, resulting in a distinct, much slower latency band.

name: Asset Class and Liquidity
description: Analyzing highly liquid 'Major' currency pairs (like EUR/USD) involves processing millions of ticks, whereas 'Exotics' (like USD/HUF) have far lower data density. The analysis duration will cluster based on the asset class currently being analyzed.

name: News and Event Volume
description: Fundamental Analysis (FA) relies on scraping and processing geopolitical news, economic calendars, and financial reports. On days with many scheduled economic releases, the amount of data to ingest and analyze spikes, leading to discrete clusters of longer processing times.

name: Dynamic Historical Lookback Window
description: The system may programmatically adjust its lookback window (e.g., 50 vs. 200 vs. 1000 candles) for technical indicators depending on the market state. These discrete window sizes result in step-like execution times.

name: API Rate Limiting and Retries
description: If external APIs (for news feeds or broker data) rate-limit the system, the workflow may execute back-off and retry logic. This introduces discrete delays (e.g., 1s, 2s, 5s pause steps) creating strict multimodal spikes in duration.

name: Heterogeneous Cloud Node Allocation
description: In cloud-native or containerized deployments, instances of the workflow might run on different virtual machine classes (e.g., some on CPU-optimized nodes, others on shared/burstable instances). This hardware heterogeneity creates distinct performance tiers.

name: Shared Infrastructure and DB Load
description: The workflow's database queries can be delayed if other services are executing heavy batch writes or reports. This resource contention groups the execution times into 'uncongested' and 'congested' database states.

name: Document Complexity and Source Type
description: For FA, the workflow may analyze different document types. Processing a short text tweet or RSS feed item is near-instant, while performing NLP/sentiment analysis on a 30-page central bank PDF report takes significantly longer, creating distinct timing modes.

name: Adaptive Algorithm Complexity
description: The workflow might branch its logic. For example, if simple indicators (like moving average crossovers) show high certainty, it finishes quickly. If they are ambiguous, it may trigger heavier ML-based pattern recognition, creating a distinct high-latency tier.

name: Workflow Concurrency and Queue Delay
description: When multiple trading signals occur simultaneously, workflow instances queue up for shared execution threads or CPU time. This queue wait time causes parallel runs to cluster around distinct latency multiples.

name: Garbage Collection and Memory Pressure
description: If the runtime environment (e.g., JVM or .NET) undergoes Stop-The-World garbage collection, workflows running during these intervals experience sudden, discrete execution delays compared to those running during clean memory cycles.

name: Trading Session Timeframe
description: The overlapping of major trading sessions (e.g., London and New York) creates systemic bursts of data throughput. Workflows executed during active overlaps run in a high-density processing mode compared to quiet Asian sessions.

name: Geographical Data Routing
description: If the workflow retrieves broker data or news from geographically distributed endpoints (e.g., New York vs. London vs. Tokyo), network round-trip times (RTT) will fall into highly distinct latency bands.

name: Day of Week Market State
description: Weekend market pauses, Monday openings, and Friday afternoon liquidity drop-offs impact historical database updates and active feed processing, causing predictable weekly variations in analysis duration.
